newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Western sanctions on Nigeria biting, ex-ruler says.
newsitem.headline: Western sanctions on Nigeria biting, ex-ruler says.

text.p: Sanctions against Nigeria are starting to bite, according to a former Nigerian ruler charged with planning the country's economic future.
The sanctions were imposed by Western nations because of Nigeria's lack of democracy and human rights.

"These sanctions are somewhat hurting," Ernest Shonekan, the former interim head of state and chairman of the Vision 2010 committee which is planning Nigeria's economic future, told a workshop of the group in Lagos on Monday.
"What is more, government-to-government contacts are precluded by at least one major power on account of the existing sanctions," he said.
The major power refers to the United States, the biggest buyer of Nigeria's main export crude oil.

Washington and the European Union banned visits to their countries by members of the Nigerian military government and also froze arms sale and official aid following the 1993 annulment of a presidential election to restore democracy.

The sanctions were reinforced in 1995 when the government of General Sani Abacha, who assumed power when Shonekan resigned as interim leader in 1993, defied international opinion and hanged nine minority rights activists including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa.
Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth which groups Britain and its former allies. The suspension has cost
Nigeria aid such as Commonwealth scholarships and other projects. European Union-assisted projects have also been affected.
Shonekan, an industrialist who has good contacts with the British establishment after his long career in the Unilever group, called for more understanding of Nigeria's problems by the West.
"First and foremost we urge patience and understanding of the international community regarding nation-building efforts by Nigeria," he said.
"What we have seen in recent times are what you can call storms in the tea cup which are not totally abnormal in the process of nation building," he added.

Abacha has promised to hand over power to an elected president next year but the opposition remains critical, pointing to continued detention of opponents including Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled vote.
Western nations have yet to fully back Abacha's programme of transition to civil rule.
